## Question 4a. Identifying the Three Most Active Bluesky Users

### Methodology

I used the `atrrr` package to collect Bluesky posts about Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime performance.

I searched using four queries: `"Bad Bunny" halftime`, `"Bad Bunny" "Super Bowl"`, `"Benito" halftime`, and `"Bad Bunny"`. The searches covered posts published from 9 to 19 February 2026.

For each query, I requested up to 1,000 posts, sorted from newest to oldest. I then removed duplicate posts using their URIs and excluded posts outside the selected dates.

To keep the data relevant, I filtered for posts mentioning Bad Bunny or Benito along with terms related to the Super Bowl or halftime performance.

Finally, I identified users by their unique DIDs and counted how many different relevant posts each user had published. I ranked the users by their post counts to find the three most active accounts.

## Question 4b. Constructing and Visualising the Directed Follower Network

### Methodology

I used the three accounts identified in Question 4(a) to build a follower network.

Using the `atrrr` package, I requested up to 50 followers and 50 accounts followed by each user through `get_followers()` and `get_follows()`. If a request failed, I allowed up to three attempts.

I then used `igraph` to create a directed network. Each node represents a Bluesky account, identified by its DID. Each arrow points from the account following someone to the account being followed. For example, an arrow from User A to User B means User A follows User B.

Before creating the graph, I removed duplicate connections and self-loops, where an account would point to itself.

I highlighted the three selected accounts in orange and displayed the other accounts in blue. I used the Fruchterman-Reingold layout to arrange the nodes in the network plot.

### R Code: Network Collection

The R code below shows how I originally collected the follower and following data from Bluesky.

I did not run the API requests again when generating the report because the data had already been collected and saved.

```{r q4b-collection-code, eval=FALSE}
library(atrrr)
library(tidyverse)
library(igraph)

top_users <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# API request with retries
safe_get <- function(actor, type, limit = 50L) {

  for (attempt in 1:3) {

    result <- tryCatch(
      {
        if (type == "followers") {
          atrrr::get_followers(
            actor = actor,
            limit = limit,
            verbose = FALSE
          )
        } else {
          atrrr::get_follows(
            actor = actor,
            limit = limit,
            verbose = FALSE
          )
        }
      },
      error = function(e) {
        message(
          actor, " / ", type, ": ",
          conditionMessage(e)
        )
        NULL
      }
    )

    if (!is.null(result)) {
      return(list(
        data = head(result, limit),
        status = "success"
      ))
    }

    Sys.sleep(2^attempt)
  }

  list(
    data = tibble(),
    status = "failed"
  )
}

edges_list <- list()
request_log <- list()

for (i in seq_len(nrow(top_users))) {

  actor <- top_users$author_did[i]
  handle <- top_users$author_handle[i]

  for (type in c("followers", "following")) {

    response <- safe_get(actor, type)
    result <- response$data

    request_log[[length(request_log) + 1]] <-
      tibble(
        actor = actor,
        handle = handle,
        type = type,
        status = response$status,
        retrieved = nrow(result)
      )

    if (
      nrow(result) == 0 ||
      !all(c("did", "actor_handle") %in% names(result))
    ) {
      next
    }

    if (type == "followers") {

      edges <- tibble(
        from = result$did,
        to = actor,
        from_handle = result$actor_handle,
        to_handle = handle
      )

    } else {

      edges <- tibble(
        from = actor,
        to = result$did,
        from_handle = handle,
        to_handle = result$actor_handle
      )
    }

    edges_list[[length(edges_list) + 1]] <- edges

    Sys.sleep(1.5)
  }
}

log_df <- bind_rows(request_log)

write_csv(
  log_df,
  "Data/q4_network_collection_log.csv"
)

if (length(edges_list) == 0) {
  stop("No network edges retrieved.")
}

edges <- bind_rows(edges_list) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(from),
    !is.na(to),
    from != to
  ) %>%
  distinct(from, to, .keep_all = TRUE)

write_csv(
  edges,
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv"
)
```

### R Code: Constructing the Directed Network

The R code below loads the saved network data and rebuilds the directed graph without making any new API requests.

```{r q4b-network-graph}
# Load original collected data
top_users <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

network_edges <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

network_log <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_collection_log.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Construct directed network
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  network_edges %>%
    dplyr::select(from, to),
  directed = TRUE
)

# Remove isolated nodes, if present
g <- igraph::delete_vertices(
  g,
  which(igraph::degree(g, mode = "all") == 0)
)

# Identify the three selected users
igraph::V(g)$is_seed <-
  igraph::V(g)$name %in% top_users$author_did

# Calculate network size
network_summary <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Nodes", "Directed edges"),
  Value = c(
    igraph::vcount(g),
    igraph::ecount(g)
  )
)
```

### Results

The network contained 196 nodes and 211 directed edges. All six API requests completed successfully.

```{r q4b-network-visualisation, fig.cap="Figure 1. Directed Bluesky follower network of the three most active accounts."}
set.seed(42)

plot(
  g,
  layout = igraph::layout_with_fr(g),
  vertex.size = ifelse(
    igraph::V(g)$is_seed, 12, 4
  ),

```

### Discussion

The network plot shows the follower and following relationships connected to the three selected accounts. I highlighted these accounts in orange to make them easier to identify.

An incoming arrow means another account follows the selected user, while an outgoing arrow means the selected user follows another account.

All three accounts had 50 followers retrieved because I limited the collection to 50 per user. The number of followed accounts differed, with 46 for `webradiomexfm.bsky.social`, 13 for `tmspn.bsky.social` and two for `chartdata.xmirror.bot`.

The graph only represents the connections collected for this analysis, rather than the full Bluesky network. I collected the follower information in November 2026, so the relationships might have changed since the February 2026 discussion.

For this reason, I treated the network as a sample of the accounts' relationships at the time of collection, rather than a complete or historical record of their connections.

## Question 4c. Degree Centrality and PageRank Analysis

### Methodology

I used the `igraph` package to calculate centrality measures for the follower network from Question 4(b), which contained 196 accounts and 211 directed connections.

I calculated four measures for each account: in-degree, out-degree, total degree and PageRank.

In-degree counts how many accounts follow a user, while out-degree counts how many accounts the user follows. Total degree combines these two values.

PageRank measures an account's importance based on its incoming connections and the importance of the accounts linking to it. I used a damping factor of 0.85.

### R Code: Centrality Calculations

```{r q4c-centrality}
library(igraph)
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load the original directed network
g <- readRDS("Data/q4_network_graph.rds")

top_users <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_top_three_users.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

edges <- read_csv(
  "Data/q4_network_edges.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# 2. Create DID-to-handle lookup
handle_lookup <- bind_rows(
  edges %>% transmute(
    did = from,
    handle = from_handle
  ),
  edges %>% transmute(
    did = to,
    handle = to_handle
  ),
  top_users %>% transmute(
    did = author_did,
    handle = author_handle
  )
) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(did),
    !is.na(handle),
    handle != ""
  ) %>%
  distinct(did, .keep_all = TRUE)

# 3. Calculate centrality measures
centrality_results <- tibble(
  did = V(g)$name,
  in_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "in"
  ),
  out_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "out"
  ),
  total_degree = degree(
    g,
    mode = "all"
  ),
  pagerank = page_rank(
    g,
    directed = TRUE,
    damping = 0.85
  )$vector
) %>%
  left_join(
    handle_lookup,
    by = "did"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    handle = coalesce(handle, did)
  ) %>%
  select(
    did,
    handle,
    in_degree,
    out_degree,
    total_degree,
    pagerank
  )

# 4. Identify highest-ranking users
top_in_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(in_degree == max(in_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_out_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(out_degree == max(out_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_total_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(total_degree == max(total_degree)) %>%
  arrange(handle)

top_pagerank <- centrality_results %>%
  filter(
    abs(pagerank - max(pagerank)) < 1e-12
  ) %>%
  arrange(handle)

# 5. Compare highest total degree and PageRank
same_top_user <- any(
  top_total_degree$did %in% top_pagerank$did
)

# 6. Create top-10 rankings
top10_degree <- centrality_results %>%
  arrange(desc(total_degree), handle) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

top10_pagerank <- centrality_results %>%
  arrange(desc(pagerank), handle) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

### Results

The three selected accounts had the same highest in-degree of 50.

```{r q4c-top-centrality}
knitr::kable(
  centrality_results %>%
    filter(did %in% top_users$author_did) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_degree)) %>%
    select(
      handle,
      in_degree,
      out_degree,
      total_degree,
      pagerank
    ),
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Table 6. Centrality Measures of the Three Selected Accounts",
  col.names = c(
    "Bluesky Account",
    "In-Degree",
    "Out-Degree",
    "Total Degree",
    "PageRank"
  )
)
```

### Highest-Ranking Accounts by Centrality Measure

```{r q4c-highest-users}
highest_users <- bind_rows(
  top_in_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "In-degree"),
  top_out_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "Out-degree"),
  top_total_degree %>%
    mutate(metric = "Total degree"),
  top_pagerank %>%
    mutate(metric = "PageRank")
) %>%
  select(
    metric,
    handle,
    in_degree,
    out_degree,
    total_degree,
    pagerank
  )

knitr::kable(
  highest_users,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Table 7. Highest-Ranking Accounts by Centrality Measure",
  col.names = c(
    "Centrality Measure",
    "Bluesky Account",
    "In-Degree",
    "Out-Degree",
    "Total Degree",
    "PageRank"
  )
)
```

`webradiomexfm.bsky.social` ranked first for out-degree with 46 connections, total degree with 96 connections and PageRank with a score of approximately 0.108.

### Comparison of Degree Centrality and PageRank

```{r q4c-degree-vs-pagerank}

  Comparison = "Highest total-degree and PageRank users overlap",

knitr::kable(
```

I also compared the accounts ranked first by total degree and PageRank. The comparison returned `TRUE`, confirming that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` ranked highest for both measures.

### Discussion

The centrality results show that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` occupied the highest-ranked position in the sampled network according to total degree and PageRank. The account had 50 incoming connections and 46 outgoing connections, giving a total degree of 96. The other two selected accounts had total degrees of 63 and 52.

Although the highest total-degree account also achieved the highest PageRank, the two measures assess different network properties. Degree centrality counts direct connections, while PageRank considers the importance of incoming connections. For example, `bsky.app` had a total degree of only two but ranked fourth by PageRank, with a score of approximately 0.0443. This demonstrates how an account with relatively few direct connections might achieve a higher PageRank through its position in the network.

The results are limited to the sampled network. In particular, the follower retrieval limit of 50 accounts per selected user affected the observed in-degree values. Therefore, the centrality rankings describe the collected network rather than the complete Bluesky network.


The results illustrate that `webradiomexfm.bsky.social` had the highest total degree and PageRank in the collected network.

This account had 50 incoming connections and 46 outgoing connections, giving a total degree of 96. The other two selected accounts had total degrees of 63 and 52.

Although the same account ranked first for both measures, degree centrality and PageRank measure different things. Degree centrality counts direct connections, while PageRank also considers the importance of accounts providing incoming connections.

For instance, `bsky.app` had only two direct connections but ranked fourth in PageRank, with a score of approximately 0.0443. This displays how an account with fewer connections might still receive a relatively high PageRank score.

These rankings only reflect the network I collected. Since I limited follower retrieval to 50 accounts per selected user, the observed in-degree values do not represent their full follower counts.

I therefore utilised these outcomes to compare the accounts within my sample rather than their overall importance across Bluesky.
